Summarize the advice given here in plain modern English.

Honey and oil and milk and butter and meat and salt and treacle and grain of all kinds and fruit and roots are all modifications of earth and water. Recluses living in the wilderness, giving up all longing (for rich and savoury food), take simple food, that is again unsavoury, for only supporting the body. After the same manner, a person that dwells in the wilderness of the world, should be ready for labour and should take food for passing through life, like a patient taking medicine. A person of noble soul, examining all things of an earthly nature that come upon him, by the aid of truth, purity, candour, a spirit of renunciation, enlightenment, courage, forgiveness, fortitude, intelligence, reflection, and austerities, and desirous of obtaining tranquillity, should restrain his senses.

All food comes from earth and water. The passage says a person should eat simply, only to keep the body going, as a patient takes medicine. A wise person who wants peace should use truth, courage, patience and self-control to rein in the senses.

I write a few lines in haste to say that I am safe—and well advanced on my voyage. This letter will reach England by a merchantman now on its homeward voyage from Archangel; more fortunate than I, who may not see my native land, perhaps, for many years. I am, however, in good spirits: my men are bold and apparently firm of purpose, nor do the floating sheets of ice that continually pass us, indicating the dangers of the region towards which we are advancing, appear to dismay them. We have already reached a very high latitude; but it is the height of summer, and although not so warm as in England, the southern gales, which blow us speedily towards those shores which I so ardently desire to attain, breathe a degree of renovating warmth which I had not expected.

A two-sentence summary of this letter, please.

Walton writes a quick letter to say he is safe and well on his way north, though he may not see England for years. His crew is brave despite the ice around them, and the summer winds are pushing them quickly forward.

Summarize this croquet scene for a child.

The chief difficulty Alice found at first was in managing her flamingo: she succeeded in getting its body tucked away, comfortably enough, under her arm, with its legs hanging down, but generally, just as she had got its neck nicely straightened out, and was going to give the hedgehog a blow with its head, it would twist itself round and look up in her face, with such a puzzled expression that she could not help bursting out laughing: and when she had got its head down, and was going to begin again, it was very provoking to find that the hedgehog had unrolled itself, and was in the act of crawling away: besides all this, there was generally a ridge or furrow in the way wherever she wanted to send the hedgehog to, and, as the doubled-up soldiers were always getting up and walking off to other parts of the ground, Alice soon came to the conclusion that it was a very difficult game indeed.

Alice tries to play croquet using a flamingo as her bat and a hedgehog as the ball. The flamingo keeps twisting round to look at her, the hedgehog crawls away, and the soldiers keep walking off. Alice decides it is a very hard game.

Summarize what happens in this meeting as bullet points.

At the panchayat meeting in Dhanauri, a seed dealer pointed to three farmers in the front row. "All three used our new wheat seed, and all three doubled their harvest!" Heads nodded. Shreya, the young agriculture extension worker, raised her hand. "How many farmers in the block bought this seed last season?" The dealer hesitated. "Around forty." "And the other thirty-seven?" Nazia, a farmer at the back, called out, "My field had the same seed. Half of it failed." Two more hands went up. Shreya kept her voice friendly. "Maybe it's a good seed. But before the panchayat praises it, let's hear from all forty, and check whose fields had canal water." The dealer's smile tightened. The three in the front row shifted in their seats.

- A seed dealer says three farmers doubled their harvest with the new seed, as proof that it is good.
- Shreya asks how many farmers bought it, and Nazia reports that half the field sown with it failed.
- Shreya suggests hearing from all forty buyers and checking who had canal water before praising the seed.

Summarize Jane's answer in two sentences.

"No," replied Jane, "I have not forgotten him; but I have nothing satisfactory to tell you. Mr. Bingley does not know the whole of his history, and is quite ignorant of the circumstances which have principally offended Mr. Darcy; but he will vouch for the good conduct, the probity and honour, of his friend, and is perfectly convinced that Mr. Wickham has deserved much less attention from Mr. Darcy than he has received; and I am sorry to say that by his account, as well as his sister's, Mr. Wickham is by no means a respectable young man. I am afraid he has been very imprudent, and has deserved to lose Mr. Darcy's regard."

Jane says Mr. Bingley does not know Wickham's whole history, but he trusts Darcy's honesty and thinks Wickham did not deserve Darcy's attention. Jane is sorry to say that, by Bingley's account, Wickham is not respectable and was reckless.

Just the main idea, please.

"It did. Bingley is most unaffectedly modest. His diffidence had prevented his depending on his own judgment in so anxious a case, but his reliance on mine made everything easy. I was obliged to confess one thing, which for a time, and not unjustly, offended him. I could not allow myself to conceal that your sister had been in town three months last winter, that I had known it, and purposely kept it from him. He was angry. But his anger, I am persuaded, lasted no longer than he remained in any doubt of your sister's sentiments. He has heartily forgiven me now."
The speaker confesses hiding the listener's sister's stay in town from Bingley, who was angry at first but has now forgiven it.

"I think that this should do," said he, glancing into the glass above the fireplace. "I only wish that you could come with me, Watson, but I fear that it won't do. I may be on the trail in this matter, or I may be following a will-o'-the-wisp, but I shall soon know which it is. I hope that I may be back in a few hours." He cut a slice of beef from the joint upon the sideboard, sandwiched it between two rounds of bread, and thrusting this rude meal into his pocket he started off upon his expedition.

Please summarize this in one line.
A man checks his looks, says he wishes Watson could come, and hurries off with a beef sandwich to follow a possible trail.

His tale is connected and told with an appearance of the simplest truth, yet I own to you that the letters of Felix and Safie, which he showed me, and the apparition of the monster seen from our ship, brought to me a greater conviction of the truth of his narrative than his asseverations, however earnest and connected. Such a monster has, then, really existence! I cannot doubt it, yet I am lost in surprise and admiration. Sometimes I endeavoured to gain from Frankenstein the particulars of his creature's formation, but on this point he was impenetrable.

Boil this down to under 55 words.

The writer believes the story mostly because of the letters of Felix and Safie and the monster seen from the ship. Although lost in surprise, the writer could not get Frankenstein to explain how the creature was made.

Wrap up this text in three sentences.

The time fixed for the beginning of their northern tour was now fast approaching; and a fortnight only was wanting of it, when a letter arrived from Mrs. Gardiner, which at once delayed its commencement and curtailed its extent. Mr. Gardiner would be prevented by business from setting out till a fortnight later in July, and must be in London again within a month; and as that left too short a period for them to go so far, and see so much as they had proposed, or at least to see it with the leisure and comfort they had built on, they were obliged to give up the Lakes, and substitute a more contracted tour; and, according to the present plan, were to go no farther northward than Derbyshire. In that county there was enough to be seen to occupy the chief of their three weeks; and to Mrs. Gardiner it had a peculiarly strong attraction. The town where she had formerly passed some years of her life, and where they were now to spend a few days, was probably as great an object of her curiosity as all the celebrated beauties of Matlock, Chatsworth, Dovedale, or the Peak.

A letter from Mrs. Gardiner delays the start of the northern tour. Business keeps Mr. Gardiner from leaving until later in July and calls him back to London within a month. So they give up the Lakes and will go only as far as Derbyshire, where Mrs. Gardiner is eager to see a town she once lived in.

Under 60 words, please: what is this excerpt about?

The pressure cooker was whistling and Mahima's mother had ten minutes before leaving for work, but she stopped stirring when Mahima muttered, "Akash says I'm stupid." "Which word hurts most?" her mother asked, turning down the flame. Mahima thought. Not "stupid". It was the way people laughed. "Why does the laughing hurt?" "Because maybe he's right." Then she frowned. "But I got full marks in spelling on Monday. So what Akash thinks isn't the truth about me. It's only his opinion." Her mother nodded and said she would phone the class teacher that evening, since grown-ups would deal with what Akash did. Mahima's chest felt lighter as the cooker whistled again.

Mahima tells her mother that Akash calls her stupid, and she realises that the laughing hurts most. She remembers her full marks in spelling and decides his words are only his opinion, and her mother says she will phone the class teacher.

In Class 4, I used to watch Sharmila Miss's face instead of the question. If she asked, 'Is a whale a fish?' I'd say 'Yes,' then see her eyebrows go up, and quickly say, 'No! Mammal!' Her face would relax, and I'd feel warm all over. Once she asked what I thought of a poem, and I waited to see if she smiled or frowned before I answered. She did neither. She just waited. I got so nervous I said, 'It's nice,' which isn't a thought at all. Afterwards she said, 'Thomas, I want to know what you think, not what you think I think.' I didn't understand then. I do a bit more now.

How would you put this paragraph in one sentence?
Thomas recalls matching answers to Sharmila Miss's face in Class 4, until she said she wanted Thomas's own thoughts.

Explain this paragraph to a little child in three sentences.

It was a quarter past six when we left Baker Street, and it still wanted ten minutes to the hour when we found ourselves in Serpentine Avenue. It was already dusk, and the lamps were just being lighted as we paced up and down in front of Briony Lodge, waiting for the coming of its occupant. The house was just such as I had pictured it from Sherlock Holmes' succinct description, but the locality appeared to be less private than I expected. On the contrary, for a small street in a quiet neighbourhood, it was remarkably animated. There was a group of shabbily dressed men smoking and laughing in a corner, a scissors-grinder with his wheel, two guardsmen who were flirting with a nurse-girl, and several well-dressed young men who were lounging up and down with cigars in their mouths.
They wait outside Briony Lodge at dusk. The house looks as Holmes described it. But the street is busier than the narrator expected.

Summarize this for a child in three sentences.

On Tuesday there was a large party assembled at Longbourn; and the two who were most anxiously expected, to the credit of their punctuality as sportsmen, were in very good time. When they repaired to the dining-room, Elizabeth eagerly watched to see whether Bingley would take the place which, in all their former parties, had belonged to him, by her sister. Her prudent mother, occupied by the same ideas, forbore to invite him to sit by herself. On entering the room, he seemed to hesitate; but Jane happened to look round, and happened to smile: it was decided. He placed himself by her.
A big party gathers at Longbourn on Tuesday. Elizabeth watches to see where Bingley will sit. He hesitates, but Jane smiles at him, and he sits by her.

Give me a summary of this text in under 60 words.

"She is a most charming young lady, indeed. Lady Catherine herself says that, in point of true beauty, Miss de Bourgh is far superior to the handsomest of her sex; because there is that in her features which marks the young woman of distinguished birth. She is unfortunately of a sickly constitution, which has prevented her making that progress in many accomplishments which she could not otherwise have failed of, as I am informed by the lady who superintended her education, and who still resides with them. But she is perfectly amiable, and often condescends to drive by my humble abode in her little phaeton and ponies."

The speaker praises Miss de Bourgh as a charming young lady, whom Lady Catherine thinks far more beautiful than other women. Her poor health has limited her skills, but she is kind and sometimes drives past the speaker's home in a small carriage.

In the Gurugram office, Imran's analytics team and Uday's sales team had to share one client dashboard. In week one, Imran sent Uday his cleaned data without being asked. Uday thanked him and sent back the client's feedback. Good. In week three, on the client call, Uday presented Imran's churn chart as "our sales insight". Imran didn't fume in the group chat or quietly stop sending data. After the call he walked to Uday's desk. "That chart was ours. Next time, credit my team, or I'll say it on the call." Uday went red. The next morning he emailed the client: "Correction: the churn analysis came from Imran's team." Imran messaged Uday privately: "Thanks. Friday's data is coming as usual." And it did.

Tell me in three sentences what this reading says.

Imran's analytics team and Uday's sales team share a client dashboard, and Imran sends Uday cleaned data. When Uday presents Imran's chart as the sales team's insight, Imran asks him to credit the analytics team next time. Uday emails the client a correction, and Imran thanks him and keeps sending data.

"'Bhishma continued, "Having said these words, the divine and puissant Narayana in the form of Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, repaired to his eternal abode of inexhaustible felicity. When, O sinless one, duties as practised by the good had such a course in days of old, what man of cleansed soul and learning is there that would disregard the Kshatriya? Like blind men lost on the way, creatures acting and abstaining unrighteously meet with destruction. O tiger among men, do thou adhere to that circle (of duties) that was first set agoing and to which the ancients had recourse. I know, O sinless one, that thou art quite competent to do this."'"

Sum up this passage for me in two sentences.

Narayana, in the form of Indra, goes to his eternal home with the Maruts. Bhishma tells the listener to keep to the duties the ancients followed, because people who act wrongly are lost like blind men on the road.

Reduce this bit of text to three sentences.

Morning dawned before I arrived at the village of Chamounix; I took no rest, but returned immediately to Geneva. Even in my own heart I could give no expression to my sensations—they weighed on me with a mountain's weight and their excess destroyed my agony beneath them. Thus I returned home, and entering the house, presented myself to the family. My haggard and wild appearance awoke intense alarm, but I answered no question, scarcely did I speak. I felt as if I were placed under a ban—as if I had no right to claim their sympathies—as if never more might I enjoy companionship with them. Yet even thus I loved them to adoration; and to save them, I resolved to dedicate myself to my most abhorred task. The prospect of such an occupation made every other circumstance of existence pass before me like a dream, and that thought only had to me the reality of life.

The narrator returns to Geneva without rest, looking so wild that the family is alarmed, but answers no questions. The narrator feels cut off from them, yet loves them dearly. To save them, the narrator commits to the hated task, which feels more real than anything else.

Give me two sentences that capture this note.

Aadhya here, writing down what I saw of my flatmate Vivek's app project this week. Until dinner on Tuesday, Vivek kept rearranging the booking screens: six tabs, then a side menu, then tabs again, muttering that every layout hid something important. Around nine he closed the laptop and said, "I'm done, I can't see it." He watched a cricket highlights video and went to bed. At breakfast he was already sketching on a napkin. "One screen," he said. "The list on top and the button fixed at the bottom. I was trying to make it hold everything. It didn't need to." I can't know what went on in his head overnight, but the fix took him ten minutes. He says sleep did the sorting.

Aadhya writes that flatmate Vivek kept rearranging his app's booking screens until he gave up for the night and went to bed. At breakfast Vivek sketched one simple screen in ten minutes, saying he had been trying to make it hold everything.

At the hostel, Varun's ID card vanished the night before exams, and he couldn't enter the hall without it. Ujjwal, his roommate, said, "Just tell the warden it's gone." Varun's hands were shaking, but he tore a page from his rough book and wrote: bag, study-hall desk, school bus, lost and found. He tipped out his bag on the bed: pens, a comb, no card. In the study hall he checked his desk, then the one beside it. At the bus bay, the conductor let him look under the seats. Nothing. Last of all, the lost-property tray at the warden's office. His card was right on top, its strap snapped.

Can you shrink this bit of text to one sentence?
When Varun's ID card goes missing the night before exams, he checks his list of places and finds it in the lost-property tray.

Distil this piece into two sentences.

Janamejaya said, "This history, O regenerate one, that I have heard from thee is exceedingly wonderful, this narration, in detail, of the installation, according to due rites, of Skanda. O thou possessed of wealth of asceticism, I deem myself cleansed by having listened to this account. My hair stands on end and my mind hath become cheerful. Having heard the history of the installation of Kumara and the destruction of the Daityas, great hath been my joy. I feel a curiosity, however, in respect of another matter. How was the Lord of the waters installed by the celestials in that tirtha in days of yore? O best of men, tell me that, for thou art possessed of great wisdom and art skilled in narration!"

Janamejaya says the account of Skanda's installation is wonderful and has left Janamejaya feeling cleansed and cheerful. Janamejaya now asks how the Lord of the waters was installed by the gods at that holy place long ago.
